title: Quantum Advantage From an Extremely Shallow Circuit
hook: A proof of quantumness you can check on a laptop, run by a quantum circuit only log-log-deep — no mid-circuit measurements, no feed-forward, just run the circuit and sample.
key_points: The task: a sampling problem easy for a shallow quantum circuit but hard for classical polynomial-time algorithms.
Hardness rests on lattice assumptions, specifically Learning With Errors (LWE).
Crucially, a purely classical computer can efficiently verify the quantum device's output.
Two implementations: log-log-depth circuits with 1- and 2-qubit gates, or constant-depth circuits with unbounded fan-in gates.
Unlike earlier low-depth proofs of quantumness, it needs no mid-circuit measurement or feed-forward.
The price is stronger, less standard assumptions — including a strengthened adaptive-hardcore-bit property of LWE.
content_html: Claiming a quantum computer did something classically impossible is easy; proving it is the hard part. A "proof of quantumness" is a task that is hard for classical machines under a standard cryptographic assumption, yet whose answers a classical verifier can check efficiently. Alexandru Gheorghiu shows such a task can be solved by a startlingly shallow quantum circuit.
extra_html: The construction compiles an earlier LWE-based single-round proof of quantumness down to very low depth, in two flavours: log-logarithmic-depth circuits built from one- and two-qubit gates, or constant-depth circuits allowed unbounded fan-in gates. The practical appeal is what it drops. Previous low-depth protocols needed mid-circuit measurements and feed-forward — measure some qubits, then apply gates conditioned on the result — which is awkward on real hardware. Here the quantum device just runs a shallow circuit and samples its output distribution. The cost, as the paper is explicit about, is stronger assumptions: a lattice knowledge assumption plus a strengthened form of LWE's adaptive-hardcore-bit property, for which the author offers supporting evidence. The conceptual takeaway is that shallow circuits already carry enough structure to do classically hard, classically checkable work.

related.title: Why Quantum Speedups Need Structure
related.hook: A long-standing conjecture says quantum computers can't beat classical ones on unstructured problems. It's now settled for parallel algorithms — and depth is the deciding resource.

related.title: Quantum Proofs Really Are More Powerful Than Classical Ones
related.hook: For 20+ years it was open whether a 'quantum-shaped' proof gives a quantum computer more power than checking an ordinary one. Researchers just found strong evidence that it does.

related.title: Qubits and Quantum Computing
related.hook: A normal bit is a 0 or a 1. A qubit can be both at once — and linking many of them lets a quantum computer explore a staggering number of possibilities together.

related.title: Proving You Really Ran the Hard Quantum Circuit
related.hook: Quantum advantage demos have a credibility gap: the circuits are hard to check. This one carries its own error-detecting certificate.

flashcards.back_html: A task a quantum device can do but a classical computer provably cannot do efficiently, whose answers a classical verifier can still check — evidence the device is really quantum.

flashcards.prompt: What makes this construction easier to run on hardware than earlier low-depth proofs of quantumness?

choices.text: It needs no mid-circuit measurements or feed-forward — just run the shallow circuit and sample
It requires no qubits at all, only classical randomness
It works without any error correction because the circuit is fault-tolerant by design

flashcards.explanation_html: Mid-circuit measurement and conditional gate application are hard on real devices. Removing them reduces the protocol to a single shallow circuit plus output sampling.

flashcards.prompt: What is the trade-off the author accepts for pushing the depth this low?
flashcards.back_html: Reliance on less standard cryptographic assumptions: a lattice knowledge assumption plus a strengthened variant of LWE's adaptive-hardcore-bit property.
